overview.title: A GPT that predicts the next token
overview.summary: A stack of causal blocks turns token ids into next-token scores, and can draw new ids one at a time.

sections.title: Size the GPT with seven numbers
sections.pseudocode:
Choose the context length, vocabulary, depth, heads, width, dropout, and whether biases are on.
The defaults match a small GPT-2: context 1024, vocabulary 50304, twelve layers, twelve heads, width 768.
# Insight: GPT-2's real vocabulary is 50257 ids, padded to a multiple of 64.

sections.title: Each block may look only left, then mixes
sections.pseudocode:
Normalize with epsilon 1e-5, let every token attend to earlier tokens, and add that back.
The query, key, and value projection is 3 times the width.
Then widen by 4, apply GELU, project back, and add that back too.
Attention scores are a scaled dot product, then softmax. Future positions stay hidden.
# Insight: Nothing in a block may read a later token. That is what makes the model causal.

sections.title: Embed ids, run the stack, score the next token
sections.pseudocode:
Add a token vector and a position vector, then run every block.
Tie the token table to the output head.
Start matrices at standard deviation 0.02, and shrink residual projections further.
Report the parameter count in millions, dividing by 1e6.
With targets, score every position and take cross-entropy.
Without targets, score only the last position.
# Insight: The loss trains the model to name the next id. Sampling only needs that last score.

sections.title: Draw one id and append it
sections.pseudocode:
Crop the context to **block_size**, score it, divide by temperature, optionally keep the top-k, and sample.
Append the id and repeat.
# Insight: The new id goes back into the context. Attention is recomputed; there is no cache.

sections.title: GPT-2 weights can be copied in
sections.pseudocode:
gpt2 is 12 layers, 12 heads, width 768 (124M). Medium is 24, 16, 1024 (350M).
Large is 36, 20, 1280 (774M). XL is 48, 25, 1600 (1558M).
Force vocabulary 50257 and context 1024.
Transpose the Conv1D matrices, then copy the rest.
# Insight: This loads an existing checkpoint. It does not train one.

sections.title: Decay matrices, and estimate speed
sections.pseudocode:
AdamW decays tensors of 2 or more dimensions, not biases or norm scales.
A flop estimate, 6 times the parameter count plus an attention term, is compared with 312e12.
# Context: 312e12 stands for an A100 bfloat16 peak. The fraction is a rough utilization, not a benchmark guarantee.

logic.title: A GPT that predicts the next token
logic.summary: Turn token ids into next-token scores, using stacked blocks that may look only at earlier tokens.

sections.title: Choose the model's sizes
sections.pseudocode:
Record how the GPT is sized.
Allow sequences of **block_size** tokens, default 1024.
Use a vocabulary of **vocab_size** ids, default 50304.
Pad GPT-2's 50257 ids up to a multiple of 64.
Stack **n_layer** blocks, default twelve.
Give each block **n_head** attention heads, default twelve.
Give each token a vector of width **n_embd**, default 768.
Drop out with probability **dropout**. The default is 0.
Keep a **bias** on linears and layer norms when asked.
# Context: These seven numbers are the whole architecture. Training and sampling pass the same config in.

sections.title: Let each token look only left
sections.pseudocode:
Build one causal self-attention layer.
Require the width to divide evenly by the head count.
Project each token into query, key, and value together.
That projection is 3 times the embedding width.
Project the mixed heads back to the embedding width.
Drop out the attention weights and the residual output.

Prefer Flash Attention when this PyTorch provides it.
Otherwise warn, and store a lower-triangular mask of ones.
The mask is **block_size** by **block_size**.

Read the batch size, the length, and the width.
Split the projection into query, key, and value.
Reshape each as batch, heads, time, then head width.
That reshape swaps axes -2 and -1, so time stays beside the head width.

If Flash Attention is available:
    Score queries against keys with a causal mask.
    Drop out attention while the module is training.
Otherwise:
    Score every query against every earlier and current key.
    Scale by $1/\sqrt{d}$, where $d$ is the head width.
    Hide future positions with negative infinity.
    Turn the scores into weights with softmax.
    Drop out those weights.
    Mix the values by the weights.

Lay the head outputs back side by side.
Project that mix, drop out, and return it.
# Why: Dividing by the square root of the head width keeps the dots from growing with that width, so softmax does not saturate.
# Insight: A token never reads a later token. The triangular mask, or is_causal, is what enforces it.

sections.title: Widen the vector, then squash it
sections.pseudocode:
Build the feed-forward layer inside a block.
Expand each token to 4 times the embedding width.
Apply GELU.
Project back to the embedding width.
Drop out.

On each token, expand, apply GELU, project back, and drop out.
Return that vector.
# Context: This mix never looks at other positions. Attention already gathered them. GELU is a smooth gate: it passes positive values and shrinks negative ones.

sections.title: Normalize, with an optional shift
sections.pseudocode:
Learn a scale for every channel.
Learn a shift too, unless bias is off.
Normalize the last dimension.
Use epsilon 1e-5 so the variance cannot be zero.
# Context: Layer norm makes each token's channels have a steady spread before attention or the feed-forward mix. The optional bias is the shift.

sections.title: Add each sublayer back onto the stream
sections.pseudocode:
In each block, normalize, then attend, then normalize, then mix.
Add the attention output back onto the input.
Add the feed-forward output back onto that.
Return the sum.
# Insight: The adds are residual connections. The block changes the stream by a delta instead of replacing it.
# Context: The first norm feeds attention. The second feeds the widen-and-squash layer. Each sublayer sees a normalized copy, and the original stream stays on the skip path.

sections.title: Stack embeddings, blocks, and a tied word head
sections.pseudocode:
Require a vocabulary size and a block size.
Keep the config.
Look up a vector per token id. Call that table **wte**.
Look up a vector per position. Call that table **wpe**.
Drop out the sum of those two.
Stack **n_layer** identical blocks.
Normalize once more at the end of the stack.
Map the final vector to one score per vocabulary id.
Call that map **lm_head**. Give it no bias.

Tie **wte** to **lm_head**. They share one matrix.
# Why: The same vectors that read token ids also score them. One table means fewer free parameters, and the input and output stay in one geometry.

Draw every linear and embedding matrix from a normal.
Use mean 0 and standard deviation 0.02.
Zero each linear bias.
Shrink residual projections by the square root of 2 times the depth.
# Context: The source applies the GPT-2 residual scale so a deep stack of adds does not start huge.

Sum the parameters.
When asked, subtract the position table.
Keep the token table, because the output head uses it.
Print the count in millions, dividing by 1e6.
# Insight: Position vectors are not shared, so they are the ones left out of the non-embedding count.

sections.title: Turn ids into scores, and a loss if targets arrived
sections.pseudocode:
Read the device, the batch, and the length.
Reject a sequence longer than **block_size**.
Number the positions from 0 up to the length.

Look up each token id and each position.
Add those vectors, then drop out.
Run every block.
Normalize the stack output.

If targets were passed:
    Score every position over the vocabulary.
    Measure cross-entropy against the targets.
    Ignore a target of -1.
Otherwise:
    Score only the last position.
    Leave the loss empty.
Return the scores and the loss.
# Insight: Training needs a score at every position. Sampling only needs the next token, so the head skips the earlier positions.
# Context: Cross-entropy here is the average negative log probability of the correct next id.

sections.title: Shrink a pretrained context
sections.pseudocode:
Refuse a context longer than the one already built.
Remember the shorter **block_size**.
Cut the position table down to it.
If a causal mask is stored, cut that too.
# Context: A GPT-2 checkpoint is built for 1024 positions. A smaller run can crop that table instead of retraining it.

sections.title: Copy OpenAI GPT-2 weights in
sections.pseudocode:
Accept only gpt2, gpt2-medium, gpt2-large, or gpt2-xl.
Allow a dropout override, and nothing else.
Load the matching Hugging Face GPT-2.

gpt2 uses 12 layers, 12 heads, and width 768. That is the 124M model.
gpt2-medium uses 24 layers, 16 heads, and width 1024. That is the 350M model.
gpt2-large uses 36 layers, 20 heads, and width 1280. That is the 774M model.
gpt2-xl uses 48 layers, 25 heads, and width 1600. That is the 1558M model.
Force vocabulary 50257, context 1024, and bias on.
If dropout was overridden, print it and use that rate.

Build a fresh GPT in that shape.
Drop the attention mask buffers. They are not parameters.
Drop the same buffers on the Hugging Face model.
Require the remaining names to match one for one.

For the attention and feed-forward matrices, transpose.
Copy every other tensor straight across.
Return the filled model.
# Why: The OpenAI checkpoint stored those matrices as Conv1D, which is transposed relative to a Linear. The copy flips them.
# Insight: This downloads the public GPT-2 checkpoint, then copies weights. It does not retrain them.

sections.title: Decay matrices, not shifts
sections.pseudocode:
Keep parameters that still receive gradients.
Decay every tensor with 2 or more dimensions.
Leave biases and layer-norm scales undecayed, at decay 0.
Print how many tensors and parameters fall in each group.
Use AdamW.
Fuse the AdamW kernel when it exists and the device is cuda.
Return that optimizer.
# Why: Decay pulls large weight matrices toward zero. Biases and norm scales are few numbers; decaying them tends to fight the normalization.

sections.title: Estimate how hard the GPU is working
sections.pseudocode:
Count the parameters.
Let the head width be the embedding divided by the head count.
Estimate flops per token as 6 times the parameter count.
Add 12 times layers, times heads, times head width, times **block_size**.
Scale by **block_size** again for a forward and backward pass.
Scale by how many sequences this step ran.
Divide by the elapsed seconds.
Compare with 312e12, which the comment calls 312 TFLOPS, an A100 bfloat16 peak.
Return that fraction.
# Context: The 6N term is the usual matmul cost of a forward and backward pass. The extra term pays for attention scores, which grow with the context length. The source points at the PaLM paper's appendix for this estimate.

sections.title: Sample the next id, then feed it back
sections.pseudocode:
Repeat for each new token you still owe.
If the context is longer than **block_size**, keep only the last **block_size** ids.
Score that context.
Keep the last position and divide by the temperature.
If a top-k was given:
    Find the k largest scores.
    Set every smaller score to negative infinity.
Turn the scores into probabilities.
Draw one id.
Append it, and repeat.
Return the full id sequence.
# Insight: Each new id is appended, and attention runs again over the whole crop. This function does not keep a key-value cache.
# Context: Temperature below 1 sharpens the distribution. top-k sets every id outside the k most likely to probability zero before the draw.
